body:
FYI, this is another version of this check that I hadn't upstreamed yet. This one uses a specific existing file instead of `-` so the process doesn't hang waiting for input. It omits the `-E` since that outputs the whole file and it isn't needed in order to grab the include paths (and less output to parse).

This isn't a totally complete solution, though; for example, cross-compilation compilers require the `--target` in order to output the correct include paths, and there might be other compilers that need other arguments. You might want to provide an optional custom environment variable that platforms can fill out with additional arguments to add to this check, to ensure the generation is actually correct.

```
def get_default_include_paths(env):
    compiler = env.subst("$CXX")
    target = os.path.join(env.Dir("#main").abspath, "main.cpp")
    args = [compiler, target, "-x", "c++", "-v"]
    ret = subprocess.run(args, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.STDOUT, text=True)
    output = ret.stdout
    match = re.search(r"#include <\.\.\.> search starts here:([\S\s]*)End of search list.", output)
    return [x.strip() for x in match[1].strip().splitlines()]
```

So this property is a property that VS usually writes to a `godot.vcxproj.user` file. This is because it's usually a property that the user often manually sets. I think it might be fine to be set here as a default, because any existing `godot.vcxproj.user` setting will override it, though. Have you tested overriding this in VS and seeing where it stores the override?
This should come before the Configuration property group, and it should happen regardless of platform toolsets (it's the same for msvc and clang and any other toolsets).
This should not exclude the clang toolset. Is this a Rider thing? There are clang toolsets for VS and this will break all of the platforms that use the clang toolset.
Same comment as above for clang toolset condition.

These should not be defined here, these are set in the per-build-target props file. The vcxproj should only be setting generic defines and properties that are not platform or build target specific, as much as possible. Any build-specific preprocessor definitions, includes, build arguments, anything like that needs to be set on the specific build target props file.

1. Why do you need to define a platform toolset here? This is a thing that is usually set by default by VS, then platform-specific configurations that ship with VS extensions set it if they need to, and users can modify it. It's probably easier for future maintenance if this block is inlined instead of including an external file. In these generated project/props files, other files are only included when they are also generated.
This nmake file isn't generated, so its contents can be inlined here directly.
This doesn't do anything, what are you trying to do here?

This condition is checking the wrong file.

One of the goals of the generation is to make sure that all essential properties are set so that VS doesn't change the vcxproj automatically on open without user action.

Since you're moving the PlatformToolset property from the vcxproj to the individual platform files, what happens when you open the vcxproj on VS for a platform+target combo with no generated props file, does VS automatically add one, modifying the vcxproj in the process?

Here is a useful breakdown of `PlatformToolset` and `DefaultPlatformToolset` and where and how they should be defined in order for VS to work properly: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/45452145/how-to-set-platformtoolset-property-from-msbuild
If the platform toolset is meant to be set to an optional default, then it might need to be defined in the Globals property block before importing the defaults and using an optional `DefaultPropertyToolset` if defined. Having it in the generated `.props` files is likely far too late in the process, as VS needs to know what the toolset is during the `Microsoft.Cpp.props` import, which is where platform-specific VS extensions are also processed.
